food.text: Hawaii's food blends Polynesian, North American and East Asian traditions. Immigrant workers came to the pineapple and sugarcane plantations between 1850 and 1930, and their foods mixed into a 'local food' style. It produced plantation plate lunches, Spam musubi and the loco moco.

Chefs refined Hawaii's local style and labeled it 'Hawaii regional cuisine' in 1991. It uses locally grown ingredients to blend all of Hawaii's historical influences into a new fusion cuisine. Well-known local restaurants serving 'Hawaiian Food' had opened shortly after World War II.

Colonialism brought canned goods to Polynesia, including the highly prized corned beef, and this changed local diets. Natural disasters brought food aid from New Zealand, Australia and the US. After the world wars of the mid-20th century, foreign foods became a bigger part of daily meals while taro and coconuts remained.

In 1960, half of the land in Hawaii was devoted to ranching for beef export, but by 1990 that share had shrunk to 25 percent. Hawaii's cowboys, the paniolos, chewed pipikaula, a salted and dried beef resembling jerky. With Asian influence, beef strips are commonly marinated in soy sauce.

Leonard's Bakery opened in Honolulu in 1952, founded by Margaret and Frank Leonard Rego Sr. Portuguese plantation workers had brought the holeless malasada to Hawaii at the turn of the 20th century, but Leonard's brought it to a wider audience. Frank's mother had encouraged him to sell them.

In 2012 the Honolulu Star-Advertiser reported that Leonard's Bakery sold over 15,000 malasadas daily, or over 160 million since its opening. Residents of other Hawaiian islands often bring them home as an omiyage, a souvenir gift.

Faraoa 'ipo is a ball bread made in the Tuamotu archipelago of French Polynesia. It is made from flour leavened with yeast, with coconut, coconut milk, sugar and salt added. The dough is shaped into a ball and cooked in coconut water, or in an earth oven wrapped in banana leaves.

Leonard Rego Jr. opened a franchise of Leonard's Bakery in Japan's Yokohama World Quarter Shopping Center in December 2008. Japanese investors first asked about licensing the brand in March 2008, and Rego felt the timing with the Great Recession 'couldn't have been more perfect'. The shop first sold only cinnamon and sugar malasadas, and later added fillings.

The Urapmin people of New Guinea engaged in cannibalism in war, eating the people they fought. They also had a system of food taboos in which dogs could not be eaten and had to be kept from breathing on food, unlike humans, who could be eaten and with whom food could be shared. In parts of Melanesia, cannibalism was still practised in the early 20th century, for reasons including retaliation, insulting an enemy people, or absorbing the dead person's qualities.

art.text: The Royal Hawaiian Hotel in Waikiki is known as "The Pink Palace of the Pacific". The nickname comes from the bright pink concrete stucco façade of its Spanish/Moorish styled architecture and its prominent spot on a wide sandy beach.

In the first half of the 20th century, Micronesia's cultural integrity declined under strong Western and Japanese Imperialist influence. A number of historical artistic traditions, especially sculptural ones, simply ceased to be practiced. Traditional architecture and weaving continued.

Contemporary Pacific art is described as alive and well. It keeps traditional styles, symbols and materials but reimagines them in a diversity of contemporary forms. These forms reveal the complexity of geographic, cultural and individual interaction and history.
By the 20th century, Melanesian art began to find its way to the West. It had a profound impact on contemporary artists there.

Hapa haole music, meaning 'half foreign' in Hawaiian, uses mostly English lyrics with Hawaiian themes and instruments like the ukulele and steel guitar. It began in the early 20th century, blending traditional Hawaiian music with American ragtime. In 1916 it was the best-selling genre in the United States.

Tiki culture is an American-originated art, music and entertainment movement inspired by Polynesian, Melanesian and Micronesian cultures. Beginning in California in the 1930s, it decorated themed bars and restaurants with tiki carvings and complex, alluringly named alcoholic drinks. Some consider it a 'fantasia of trans-Pacific cultures' and 'colonial nostalgia', lumping together many unrelated Pacific cultures, religions and languages. Its appropriation of indigenous Pacific cultures is increasingly challenged as culturally insensitive or racist, and some critics say it diverts attention from the history of violent colonialism in the region.

In the second half of the 20th century, independence from colonial powers let Micronesia's traditional arts find renewed interest and respect from within the region. A new generation was taught these art forms. Toward the end of the century there was also a notable movement of contemporary art in Micronesia.

The Royal Hawaiian was designed by the acclaimed New York firm of Warren and Wetmore. The sprawling pink stucco complex cost over $4 million at 1927 prices and was surrounded by a 15-acre landscaped garden. Its H-shaped layout held 400 rooms, each with bath and balcony.

The song 'My Waikiki Mermaid', possibly the first hapa haole song, was composed by Sonny Cunha in 1903. Hapa haole reached the mainland United States at several points in the 1910s, including the 1912 Broadway musical The Bird of Paradise. Bands also played it at the Hawaiian Pavilion of the Panama–Pacific International Exposition in 1915.

A great cultural disruption followed the Second World War in Melanesia, and much traditional art began to decline or be destroyed. Decades later, this was followed by a newfound appreciation for the region's native art forms.

In 1925, the Matson Line partnered with Castle & Cooke on a "grand scheme" to make Hawaii a luxury destination. It called for the ocean liner SS Malolo, a luxury beach resort hotel for its passengers, and the Waialae Country Club for the hotel's guests. The hotel became the Royal Hawaiian.

Harry Owens' 'Sweet Leilani' became a number one hit in the United States after Bing Crosby performed it in the 1937 film Waikiki Wedding. The song won the Academy Award for Best Original Song in 1938. It came as the hapa haole craze was peaking and beginning to fade in the 1930s.

Matson and Castle & Cooke had never operated hotels, so they bought the Territorial Hotel Company to run the new Royal Hawaiian. They then demolished the company's Honolulu Seaside Hotel and built the new hotel on its site.

The Royal Hawaiian closed on June 1, 2008, for renovation and reopened on January 20, 2009, as a member of The Luxury Collection. An extended renovation of the Royal Beach Tower was completed in 2010.

war.text: Between 1966 and 1996, the French Government conducted 193 surface and underwater nuclear bomb tests at the atolls of Moruroa and Fangataufa. The last test was conducted on 27 January 1996. After the Centaure test over Mururoa Atoll on 17 July 1974, the atomic cloud and fallout did not go in the planned direction and reached Tahiti and the surrounding islands 42 hours later. As many as 111,000 people were affected, and reports showed that some people on Tahiti were exposed to 500 times the maximum allowed level for plutonium.

On 22 September 1914, during World War I, the German armoured cruisers SMS Scharnhorst and Gneisenau entered the port of Papeete on Tahiti and shelled the town and its fortifications. French shore batteries and a gunboat resisted but were greatly outgunned and scored no hits. The Germans finished off the French gunboat Zélée and the freighter Walküre, which were still afloat despite the French scuttling attempts. The shelling set the town on fire, burning two entire blocks to the ground, and killed a Japanese civilian and a Polynesian boy, while there were no military casualties on either side.

Wake Island was the site of a pitched World War II battle in 1941. Midway Atoll was the center of a major battle of WWII that helped turn the tide of the Pacific War. Both remote islands are part of the United States Minor Outlying Islands.

The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, in south-central Oahu, Hawaii, was the critical attack that brought the United States into World War II. During the war, a number of Polynesian islands played critical roles.

The main German objective at Papeete was to seize the coal piles stored on the island. The French destroyed the coal at the start of the action, so the Germans were denied their primary objective of replenishing their own stocks.

On 5 September 1995 the government of Jacques Chirac conducted the first of a series of nuclear test detonations off the shores of Moruroa. A resulting riot in Papeete lasted two days, damaged the international airport and injured 40 people. Similar rioting had followed another French test in 1987.

The raid on Papeete revealed the German cruisers' positions to the British Admiralty. This let the Admiralty inform Rear Admiral Christopher Cradock of the German intentions, which led to the Battle of Coronel, where the entire German East Asia Squadron defeated a Royal Navy squadron.

The hundreds of shells fired by Spee's ships at Papeete were irreplaceable. This depletion of ammunition contributed to the German East Asia Squadron's failure to adequately defend itself against British battlecruisers at the Battle of the Falkland Islands.
Johnston Atoll was a famous island for its Cold War base, which was expanded and used to destroy chemical weapon stockpiles. It was also the site of a nuclear accident.

Lieutenant Destremau was chastised by his misinformed superior for his defense of Papeete and the loss of the gunboat Zélée. He was summoned back to Toulon under arrest to be court-martialled but died of illness in 1915. In 1918 he was posthumously awarded the Légion d'honneur.

After withdrawing from Papeete, Scharnhorst and Gneisenau rendezvoused with Nürnberg and Titania at Nuku Hiva. There they resupplied and the crews took shore leave before moving on to meet the rest of the squadron at Easter Island.

literature.text: When Robert Dean Frisbie began writing about Polynesia, he followed in the footsteps of other famous 19th century South Sea writers. One of his major influences was Robert Louis Stevenson, and he kept in touch with fellow travel writers of his own time.

Robert Dean Frisbie was an American writer of travel literature about Polynesia. His first complete narrative, The Book of Puka-Puka, was published in 1929. It told of his search for solitude on the far-flung Northern Cook atoll of Pukapuka.

In the 1940s, after the death of Frisbie's wife, the family visited the uninhabited Northern Cook atoll Suwarrow and lived there for almost a year. They survived a hurricane on a tiny islet there. The celebrated story was serialized in the Atlantic Monthly in 1943 as The Story of an Island: Marooned by Request, and later appeared in his memoir The Island of Desire.

The 2023 children's book Brave Mrs. Sato, written by Lori Matsukawa and illustrated by Tammy Yee, tells of a picture bride who emigrated from Japan to Hawaii. She befriends a young girl and teaches her about her Japanese heritage and her experiences as a picture bride. The book is based upon the author's real-life experiences with her own babysitter.

James A. Michener's novel Hawaii was published in 1959, the year Hawaii became the 50th U.S. state, and has been translated into 32 languages. It follows the original Hawaiians, the early American missionaries and merchants, and Chinese and Japanese immigrants. In it, the Bora Boran king Tamatoa and his brother Teroro flee the demands of the fire god 'Oro, who constantly demands human sacrifices, and Teroro secretly sets fire to Havaiki in revenge. The patriarch of the Kee family contracts leprosy and is sent to the leper colony in Molokai. A 1966 film starred Max von Sydow and Julie Andrews.

In Tahiti, Frisbie met Charles Nordhoff and James Norman Hall, well-known co-authors of the Mutiny on the Bounty series. Meeting them encouraged him to write his first complete narrative, which marked the starting point of his writing career.

Tom Neale, a loner, was inspired by Frisbie's tales of isolation on Suwarrow. He lived alone on the atoll on three occasions, in 1952 to 1954, 1960 to 1964 and 1967 to 1977. He wrote a book about it in which he credits Frisbie as his inspiration.

Frisbie's daughter Florence, better known as Johnny, was born in Papeete, Tahiti, in 1932. Encouraged by her father, she kept journals in three languages, including Pukapukan. At age 12 she began the autobiographical children's novel Miss Ulysses of Puka-Puka, published by Macmillan in 1948.

After returning from his second stay on Suwarrow in 1964, Tom Neale wrote An Island to Myself, published by Doubleday in 1966. In Great Britain it was republished the same year by Collins under a slightly different title, An Island to Oneself.
After her father's death in 1948, Johnny Frisbie wrote another book about her family, The Frisbies of the South Seas. It was published by Doubleday in 1959.
tags: The Frisbies of the South Seas

literature.text: In 1943, Frisbie was diagnosed with tuberculosis and evacuated by then U.S. Navy Lieutenant James Michener to a hospital on American Samoa. His recovery was spotty, but he continued to travel, write and publish until his death at age 52, on November 18 (or 19), 1948, in Avatiu, Cook Islands, from an apparent tetanus infection.

Da Jesus Book, a Hawaii Pidgin translation of the New Testament, was published by Wycliffe Bible Translators in 2000. Retired Cornell linguistics professor Joseph Grimes worked with 27 pidgin speakers for 12 years to produce the 752-page book. The Old Testament translation was completed in 2020.
literature.source_title: Bible translations into the languages of Hawaii

literature.text: Frisbie met 16-year-old Ngatokorua, also known as Inangaro, on Pukapuka and married her in 1928 on Penrhyn. She became the mother of their five children. In 1930 the family sailed back to Tahiti, where he began his second autobiography, My Tahiti, published in 1937. He also began another book, A Child of Tahiti, which was never published.

Frisbie's first published article was Fei-hunting in Polynesia, which appeared in Forum in 1923. He went on to produce a great number of sketches, articles and books printed by several publishers in America.

The Hawaiian Bible, Ka Baibala Hemolele, was published in 2018 in print and electronic forms. It uses the 19th-century Hawaiian text, re-edited in modern Hawaiian orthography with diacritical marks such as ʻOkina and Kahakō. The project was supported by Partners In Development Foundation.

science.text: In 1947, Thor Heyerdahl drifted 8,000 km across the Pacific Ocean on a primitive hand-built raft from South America to the Tuamotu Islands. The Kon-Tiki expedition was meant to show that South Americans could have colonized Polynesia first, though the scientific community had widely rejected his ideas even before it sailed.

Isabella Aiona Abbott was the first native Hawaiian woman to receive a PhD in science, and she became a leading expert on Pacific marine algae. She earned her doctorate in botany from the University of California, Berkeley in 1950.

Frank Der Yuen, an American aeronautical engineer who lived in Honolulu, invented the jet bridge, also called the passenger boarding bridge. He graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1933.

The 1976 voyage of the Hōkūleʻa from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti was partly a demonstration to prove Heyerdahl wrong. This replica of a Polynesian double-hulled voyaging canoe sailed against prevailing winds using only wayfinding and celestial Polynesian navigation, unlike the modern equipment and charts of the Kon-Tiki.

NELHA, the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaii Authority, is a 675-acre ocean science and technology park on the west side of the island of Hawaiʻi. Its tenants, including microalgae farms, aquaculture and solar technology, can draw on pipelines delivering deep-sea water from a depth of up to 3,000 feet.
The Hōkūleʻa remains fully operational and has since completed ten other voyages. These include a three-year circumnavigation of the planet from 2014 to 2017, made with sister ships.

A 2020 study found that Polynesians and the Indigenous peoples of South America came in contact around 1200 AD, centuries before Europeans interacted with either group. Genetic evidence of this kind offers a modern scientific counterpoint to Heyerdahl's idea of one-way voyages from South America.

politics.text: German-controlled Western Samoa was occupied by New Zealand in World War I and later administered under a Class C League of Nations mandate. After repeated efforts by the Samoan independence movement, the Western Samoa Act of 24 November 1961 granted independence, effective January 1, 1962.

French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France and its sole overseas country. The United Nations still classifies it as a non-self-governing territory. It is spread across 121 islands and atolls in the South Pacific.

In 1993, the 100th anniversary of the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom, Congress passed the Apology Resolution and President Bill Clinton signed it into law. It apologized to Native Hawaiians on behalf of the United States for its involvement in the overthrow. The source calls it one of the few times the U.S. government has formally apologized for its actions.

Tonga became a British protectorate under a Treaty of Friendship on 18 May 1900, at a time when European settlers and rival Tongan chiefs were trying to oust the second king. Despite the protectorate, Tonga kept its monarchy and most of its local laws without interruption, with Britain exerting varying influence through consuls appointed by the Western Pacific High Commission. On June 4, 1970, the Kingdom of Tonga became independent from the British Empire.

Swedish anthropologist Bengt Danielsson, a crew member on the 1947 Kon-Tiki expedition, settled in French Polynesia. He and his wife Marie-Thérèse were outspoken critics of French nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa atolls. In 1991 they received the Right Livelihood Award for their campaigning.
Fiji, which Cakobau had ceded to the United Kingdom in 1873 while heavily indebted to foreign creditors, became independent on 10 October 1970. It then became a republic on 28 September 1987.

An organic law of 12 April 1996 states that French is the official language of French Polynesia, while Tahitian and other Polynesian languages can be used. At the 2017 census, 73.9% of people aged 15 and older spoke French most at home, up from 68.6% in 2007.

The new Independent State of Samoa was not a monarchy, though the Malietoa titleholder remained very influential. That effectively ended with the death of Malietoa Tanumafili II, the country's head of state, on May 11, 2007.

Bengt and Marie-Thérèse Danielsson wrote Poisoned Reign: French Nuclear Colonialism in the Pacific, published in 1986. Bengt's 1991 Right Livelihood Award citation praised him for exposing the tragic results of French nuclear colonialism and advocating an end to it.

The Apology Resolution concedes that the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaii involved the active participation of agents and citizens of the United States. It also says Native Hawaiians never directly relinquished their claims to sovereignty. Debates over the event play an important role in the Hawaiian sovereignty movement.

The tafaʻifa system dominated Samoan politics well into the 20th century. It was disrupted in the early 1900s by colonial intervention, including an east-west division under the Tripartite Convention of 1899 and annexation by the German Empire and the United States.
In 2013, Hawaii became the fifteenth U.S. state to legalize same-sex marriage. The change reportedly boosted tourism by $217 million.
Native Hawaiian cultural practitioners have repeatedly failed in court to prove that their practices at Mauna Kea predate 1893. That year is the threshold for protection under Hawaii State law.

philosophy.text: Hoʻoponopono is a traditional Hawaiian practice of reconciliation and forgiveness. Similar forgiveness practices are performed on islands throughout the South Pacific, including Samoa, Tahiti and New Zealand. Mary Kawena Pukui, born in 1895, first recorded her childhood experiences of it in her 1958 book.

Hawaiian religion is polytheistic, with many deities and spirits, including the animistic belief that spirits are found in animals and natural elements such as the waves and the sky. Prominent deities include Kāne, Kū, Lono and Kanaloa. Today its practices are protected by the American Indian Religious Freedom Act.

Since 2014, protests have taken place on the Island of Hawaii over choosing Mauna Kea as the site of the Thirty Meter Telescope. Some Hawaiians regard Mauna Kea as the most sacred mountain of Native Hawaiian religion and culture. The protests went global within weeks of the April 2, 2015 arrest of 31 people blockading the road.

Psychologist Dr. Ihaleakala Hew Len took his first class with Morrnah Simeona in 1982 and trained as her instructor. After Simeona died in 1992, he returned to Hawaii to continue work in Hoʻoponopono. In 2007 he co-authored Zero Limits with Joe Vitale, referring to Simeona's teachings.

culture.text: Marriage ceremonies are important Samoan cultural events involving the transfer of the woman's property, the toga, and the man's property, the oloa. It is a village event with two ceremonies and a feast at the end. After the wedding, the newlyweds choose which side of the family to live with.

The first mosque in French Polynesia was inaugurated in Papeete, Tahiti, on 15 October 2013, during Eid al-Adha. Hundreds of Christian French Polynesians protested in the streets, and the mosque had to close over security concerns. The city authorities then allowed the building to be used only as an office.

Thor Heyerdahl's 1947 Kon-Tiki expedition, followed by a book in 1948 and a movie in 1950, injected the word 'tiki' into the popular American lexicon. Hawaiians had not used the word 'tiki', but rather 'kiʻi'. His book Aku-Aku also made the Easter Island statues, or moai, iconic.

The Honolulu Parks and Recreation Department held a pageantry in 1921 while President Woodrow Wilson was visiting Hawaii. He saw the play and said there should be more investment in traditional Hawaiian games. This is credited with leading to a renewal of pāʻani in the 1950s.

Islam is a minority religion in French Polynesia, with about 500 Muslims, mostly on Tahiti. The first mosque was inaugurated in Papeete on 15 October 2013 during Eid al-Adha, at the initiative of imam Hicham el-Berkani. Protesters numbering in the hundreds took to the streets, and the building was later permitted to be used solely as an office.

Lele koali is a Hawaiian swinging game based around either a koali vine or a koali hao, a metal chain. Unlike most pāʻani, it does not emphasize language and chanting. According to Manaleo 'Aunty' Alice, play and exchange of words can span a few days or a whole week, when everybody gathers to tell stories, play music and share meals.

The Tahiti national team reached the semifinals of the 2013 FIFA Beach Soccer World Cup, which Tahiti hosted in September 2013. They did even better in the 2015 and 2017 editions, reaching the final on both occasions.
